items.title: A client with crushing substernal pressure has diaphoresis and nausea. The pain began 20 minutes ago. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
items.content: Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly.
items.rationale: A rapid ECG identifies ischemic changes and supports time-sensitive acute coronary syndrome treatment. Do not delay assessment for routine tasks.

items.title: A client develops sudden aphasia and right arm weakness while eating breakfast. Which information is most important to establish immediately?
items.content: The exact time the client was last known to be at baseline.
items.rationale: Last-known-well time determines eligibility for time-dependent stroke interventions. Activate the stroke response and obtain urgent brain imaging.

items.title: A client with chronic kidney disease has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves. Which prescribed intervention should the nurse anticipate first to stabilize the myocardium?
items.content: IV calcium gluconate.
items.rationale: IV calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane in severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes. It does not lower serum potassium, so potassium-shifting and removal therapies are also required.

items.title: A client with heart failure is sitting upright, gasping, and producing pink frothy sputum. SpO₂ is 82%. Which action is the priority?
items.content: Activate emergency assistance and support oxygenation while preparing prescribed ventilatory support.
items.rationale: Severe hypoxemia and pulmonary edema are immediately life-threatening. Rapid escalation and respiratory support take priority while prescribed therapies are prepared.

items.title: A client is prescribed insulin lispro before meals. The meal tray is delayed and the insulin has not yet been administered. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Wait until the meal is available and coordinate administration with food intake.
items.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin has an early onset. Giving it without food increases hypoglycemia risk; coordinate administration with the meal and prescription.

items.title: Before administering digoxin to an adult, the nurse notes an apical pulse of 52/min and new nausea. What is the best action?
items.content: Withhold the dose and notify the prescriber.
items.rationale: Bradycardia and new gastrointestinal symptoms may indicate digoxin effect or toxicity. Withhold and obtain further assessment, including potassium, renal function, and drug level as ordered.

items.title: Immediately after rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate falls to 70/min and a loop of cord is visible. What should the nurse do first?
items.content: Call for emergency assistance and manually elevate the presenting part off the cord.
items.rationale: Cord compression compromises fetal oxygenation. Relieve pressure on the cord, position to reduce compression, and prepare for emergency birth.

items.title: During birth, the fetal head delivers and then retracts against the perineum. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Assist with the McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure as directed.
items.rationale: The turtle sign suggests shoulder dystocia. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure are first-line maneuvers; fundal pressure is contraindicated.

items.title: A 4-year-old has drooling, a muffled voice, tripod positioning, and inspiratory stridor. Which action should the nurse avoid?
items.content: Inspecting the throat with a tongue depressor.
items.rationale: Throat manipulation can precipitate complete airway obstruction in suspected epiglottitis. Keep the child calm and obtain expert airway support.

items.title: A client with acute mania is pacing, interrupting others, and has eaten very little. Which intervention is most appropriate?
items.content: Offer frequent high-calorie finger foods and fluids in a low-stimulation setting.
items.rationale: Finger foods support intake when sitting for meals is difficult. Reduce stimulation and provide concise limits and close safety monitoring.

items.title: Fifteen minutes after a transfusion begins, a client reports chills and flank pain. What should the nurse do immediately?
items.content: Stop the transfusion.
items.rationale: Chills and flank pain may indicate an acute hemolytic reaction. Stop the blood product, maintain IV access with normal saline using new tubing, assess, and notify the team and blood bank.

items.title: A chest drainage system becomes disconnected from the chest tube. Which immediate action should the nurse take?
items.content: Place the end of the chest tube in sterile water while obtaining a new drainage system.
items.rationale: A temporary sterile-water seal limits air entry into the pleural space. Re-establish a closed drainage system promptly and assess respiratory status.

items.title: A client receiving IV unfractionated heparin develops hematuria and a markedly elevated aPTT. What is the priority nursing action?
items.content: Stop the infusion and notify the prescriber immediately.
items.rationale: Active bleeding with excessive anticoagulation requires stopping heparin and urgent evaluation. Protamine may be prescribed for reversal depending on severity.

items.title: A client with suspected infection has BP 82/44 mm Hg, lactate 4.6 mmol/L, and altered mentation. Which action is most appropriate?
items.content: Initiate the sepsis response and administer prescribed crystalloid resuscitation promptly.
items.rationale: Hypotension, elevated lactate, and altered mentation indicate impaired perfusion. Rapid protocol-based resuscitation, cultures when feasible without delaying antimicrobials, and antibiotics are time-critical.

items.title: A client receiving hemodialysis reports that the usual vibration over the fistula is absent. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Notify the dialysis team immediately and avoid using the access until evaluated.
items.rationale: An absent thrill may indicate thrombosis or access occlusion. Prompt evaluation is needed; do not compress, puncture, or use the access.

items.title: A client with COPD has increased dyspnea, purulent sputum, and wheezing. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Position upright; administer prescribed short-acting bronchodilator; titrate prescribed oxygen to the individualized target; reassess work of breathing and oxygenation.
items.rationale: Upright positioning improves ventilation. Bronchodilation and carefully titrated oxygen treat exacerbation and hypoxemia. Reassessment detects fatigue or deterioration; oxygen should not be withheld.

items.title: A client is starting lisinopril. Which findings should the nurse teach the client to report promptly? Select all that apply.
items.content: Swelling of the lips or tongue; persistent troublesome cough; dizziness or fainting.
items.rationale: Angioedema is an emergency, cough is a recognized adverse effect, and symptomatic hypotension needs evaluation. Do not stop or change therapy without prescriber guidance unless emergency instructions apply.

items.title: A postpartum client has a boggy fundus, heavy lochia, and a rising heart rate. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
items.content: Massage the fundus; call for assistance; quantify blood loss and assess vital signs; prepare prescribed uterotonic medication.
items.rationale: Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Immediate fundal massage, escalation, quantified blood loss, hemodynamic assessment, and uterotonics are appropriate.

items.title: An infant has vomiting and diarrhea. Which findings support significant dehydration? Select all that apply.
items.content: Sunken fontanel; capillary refill of 4 seconds; markedly decreased wet diapers; lethargy.
items.rationale: These findings indicate reduced circulating volume and possible impaired perfusion. Assess severity promptly and initiate prescribed rehydration and monitoring.

items.title: A client states, “I have the pills at home and plan to take them tonight.” Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Ask directly about intent and access; maintain continuous observation per policy; remove access to potential means in the care setting; arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation.
items.rationale: A specific plan, means, and near-term timing indicate imminent risk. Direct assessment, observation, means safety, and urgent team escalation are required; do not promise secrecy.

items.title: A client has suspected C. difficile diarrhea. Which infection-control actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Use gown and gloves on room entry; wash hands with soap and water; dedicate equipment when possible; use an approved sporicidal environmental disinfectant.
items.rationale: Contact precautions and spore-focused environmental cleaning are required. Soap-and-water handwashing is preferred because alcohol hand rub does not reliably remove spores.

items.title: A client with acute pancreatitis has severe epigastric pain and vomiting. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Administer prescribed IV fluids; provide prescribed analgesia; monitor glucose and electrolytes; maintain prescribed bowel rest during severe symptoms.
items.rationale: Fluid resuscitation, pain control, and monitoring for metabolic complications are central. Oral intake is individualized and restarted as tolerated rather than prolonged automatically.

items.title: A client taking lithium reports diarrhea and develops coarse tremor and unsteady gait. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Withhold lithium pending urgent prescriber direction; assess neurologic status and hydration; obtain serum lithium and renal/electrolyte studies as ordered.
items.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms with coarse tremor and ataxia suggest toxicity. Hold further doses pending urgent review and evaluate level, renal function, electrolytes, and volume status.

items.title: A postoperative client suddenly develops pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, and SpO₂ 86%. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Activate rapid response; provide oxygen as prescribed; keep the client at rest; prepare for urgent diagnostic evaluation and anticoagulation if prescribed.
items.rationale: Acute pulmonary embolism can cause rapid hemodynamic compromise. Escalation, oxygenation, minimizing exertion, and urgent evaluation are priorities.

items.title: A pregnant client at 34 weeks has BP 168/112 mm Hg, severe headache, and visual spots. Which actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Institute seizure precautions; notify the obstetric team urgently; administer prescribed magnesium sulfate; prepare prescribed rapid-acting antihypertensive therapy.
items.rationale: Severe-range hypertension with neurologic symptoms is an obstetric emergency. Magnesium prevents seizures, while antihypertensive treatment reduces maternal stroke risk.

items.title: Twenty minutes after IV hydromorphone, a client is difficult to arouse, has RR 7/min, and SpO₂ 86%. Select the 3 priority nursing actions.
items.content: Support airway and ventilation; activate urgent clinical assistance; prepare and administer prescribed naloxone according to protocol.
items.rationale: The client has opioid-induced respiratory depression. Airway and ventilatory support, immediate escalation, and naloxone when indicated address the immediate threat; reassess for recurrent sedation.

items.title: A client with septic shock has falling urine output and rising creatinine. Select the 3 assessments most useful for evaluating renal perfusion and injury.
items.content: Hourly urine output; serial serum creatinine and electrolytes; blood pressure and perfusion trend.
items.rationale: Urine output and creatinine trends identify worsening kidney function, while hemodynamic data help assess perfusion. Interpret findings with fluid balance and clinical status.

items.title: A school-age child has severe asthma symptoms. Select the 3 findings that indicate impending respiratory failure.
items.content: Silent or markedly diminished breath sounds; decreasing level of consciousness; exhaustion with decreasing respiratory effort.
items.rationale: A silent chest may reflect critically poor airflow. Altered consciousness and exhaustion signal respiratory muscle fatigue and impending failure, requiring emergency escalation.

items.title: The RN is assigning care for stable clients. Select the 3 tasks appropriate for trained UAP personnel.
items.content: Obtain routine vital signs for a stable client; assist a stable client with bathing; record oral intake for a client without swallowing precautions.
items.rationale: Predictable, routine tasks may be delegated with clear directions and follow-up. Assessment, clinical judgment, teaching, and evaluation remain RN responsibilities.

items.title: A client with traumatic brain injury is being monitored. Select the 3 findings most concerning for rising intracranial pressure.
items.content: Declining level of consciousness; new unequal pupils; repeated vomiting with worsening headache.
items.rationale: A change in consciousness is often an early sensitive sign. Pupillary changes and worsening headache/vomiting suggest neurologic deterioration and require urgent escalation.

items.title: Match each medication with the adverse effect that requires urgent follow-up.
items.content: rows:digoxin;warfarin;gentamicin|columns:bradycardia with visual halos;melena with weakness;new tinnitus and rising creatinine|answers:digoxin=bradycardia with visual halos;warfarin=melena with weakness;gentamicin=new tinnitus and rising creatinine
items.rationale: Digoxin toxicity can cause bradycardia and visual disturbances. Warfarin-associated gastrointestinal bleeding may present as melena and weakness. Gentamicin can cause ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity.

items.title: Match each laboratory result with its most likely immediate risk.
items.content: rows:K 2.7 mEq/L;Na 118 mEq/L;Ca 7.1 mg/dL|columns:ventricular dysrhythmia;seizure from cerebral edema;tetany and laryngospasm|answers:K 2.7 mEq/L=ventricular dysrhythmia;Na 118 mEq/L=seizure from cerebral edema;Ca 7.1 mg/dL=tetany and laryngospasm
items.rationale: Severe hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk. Severe hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema and seizures. Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause tetany or laryngospasm.

items.title: For each condition, select all appropriate precautions or controls.
items.content: rows:pulmonary tuberculosis;C. difficile;influenza|columns:airborne isolation;fit-tested respirator;gown and gloves;soap-and-water hand hygiene;droplet precautions|answers:pulmonary tuberculosis=airborne isolation,fit-tested respirator;C. difficile=gown and gloves,soap-and-water hand hygiene;influenza=droplet precautions
items.rationale: Tuberculosis requires airborne isolation and fit-tested respiratory protection. C. difficile requires contact precautions and soap-and-water hand hygiene. Influenza generally requires droplet precautions.

items.title: For each fetal monitoring finding, select all appropriate interpretations or responses.
items.content: rows:recurrent late decelerations;recurrent variable decelerations;prolonged deceleration|columns:uteroplacental insufficiency concern;cord compression concern;immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation|answers:recurrent late decelerations=uteroplacental insufficiency concern,immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation;recurrent variable decelerations=cord compression concern,immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation;prolonged deceleration=immediate intrauterine resuscitation and evaluation
items.rationale: Late decelerations suggest impaired uteroplacental exchange; variable decelerations commonly reflect cord compression. A prolonged deceleration requires immediate assessment and corrective measures while preparing escalation.

items.title: Complete the initial DKA safety plan: begin prescribed ___ resuscitation; check serum ___ before insulin; if potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L, replace potassium and ___ insulin temporarily.
items.content: isotonic crystalloid|potassium|delay
items.rationale: DKA causes profound volume depletion and total-body potassium loss. Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly; severe hypokalemia must be corrected before insulin is initiated to reduce dysrhythmia risk.

items.title: A client taking warfarin should keep dietary vitamin K intake ___, report ___ stools promptly, and avoid starting NSAIDs without prescriber advice because of increased ___ risk.
items.content: consistent|black tarry|bleeding
items.rationale: Stable vitamin K intake supports predictable anticoagulation. Melena may indicate gastrointestinal bleeding. NSAIDs increase bleeding risk when combined with warfarin.

items.title: A client with pneumonia has fever, confusion, BP 78/42 mm Hg, and lactate 5.1 mmol/L. Select the likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:septic shock|actions:obtain blood cultures if this does not delay antimicrobials;administer prescribed broad-spectrum antimicrobials promptly|monitor:mean arterial pressure;serum lactate trend
items.rationale: Hypotension, altered mentation, infection, and elevated lactate indicate septic shock with impaired perfusion. Cultures should not delay antimicrobials. MAP and lactate trends help evaluate perfusion and response.

items.title: A client 30 minutes after birth has a boggy uterus, heavy bleeding, HR 128/min, and BP 86/50 mm Hg. Select the likely condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:uterine atony with postpartum hemorrhage|actions:perform fundal massage and summon help;prepare prescribed uterotonic and IV resuscitation|monitor:quantified blood loss;heart rate and blood pressure trend
items.rationale: A boggy uterus with heavy bleeding and hemodynamic changes indicates postpartum hemorrhage, commonly from atony. Immediate uterine massage, escalation, uterotonics, resuscitation, and quantified monitoring are essential.

items.title: Highlight the findings that indicate a possible acute stroke: sudden facial asymmetry; chronic bilateral knee pain; new slurred speech; unilateral arm drift; longstanding corrected visual acuity.
items.content: segments:sudden facial asymmetry|chronic bilateral knee pain|new slurred speech|unilateral arm drift|longstanding corrected visual acuity|correct:1,3,4
items.rationale: Sudden facial asymmetry, speech disturbance, and unilateral weakness are focal neurologic deficits. Activate the stroke pathway and establish last-known-well time.

items.title: Highlight the findings that require immediate escalation in a child with respiratory illness: nasal flaring; mild clear rhinorrhea; intercostal retractions; SpO₂ 87% on room air; playful behavior between coughing episodes.
items.content: segments:nasal flaring|mild clear rhinorrhea|intercostal retractions|SpO2 87% on room air|playful behavior between coughing episodes|correct:1,3,4
items.rationale: Nasal flaring, retractions, and hypoxemia indicate increased work of breathing and impaired oxygenation. The child needs prompt respiratory assessment and escalation.

items.title: A child weighs 16 kg. The prescribed medication dose is 12 mg/kg per dose. Calculate the dose in mg.
items.rationale: 12 mg/kg × 16 kg = 192 mg per dose. Verify the medication’s maximum dose, concentration, and safe pediatric dosing range before administration.

items.title: A prescription is to infuse 1,000 mL over 8 hours using an electronic pump. What rate should the nurse program in mL/hr?
items.rationale: 1,000 mL ÷ 8 hours = 125 mL/hr. Verify the order, fluid, access, and pump settings independently according to policy.

items.title: Place the actions in order for a client who develops fever, chills, and back pain during a red blood cell transfusion.
items.content: Stop the transfusion.|Keep IV access open with normal saline using new tubing.|Assess vital signs and notify the provider and blood bank.|Send the blood product and obtain ordered specimens per policy.
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion is the first action. Maintain access with new tubing and saline, assess and notify the team, then complete the reaction workup and documentation.

items.title: A client with suspected acute coronary syndrome reports ongoing chest pressure. Select all appropriate immediate nursing actions.
items.content: Obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly.|Assess vital signs and oxygenation.|Establish IV access and obtain ordered cardiac biomarkers.|Administer prescribed antiplatelet therapy after checking contraindications.|Encourage the client to walk to reduce anxiety.
items.rationale: Rapid ECG, focused assessment, IV access, biomarkers, and prescribed antiplatelet therapy support time-sensitive care. Ambulation during active ischemic symptoms is unsafe.

items.title: A client's observations trend as follows: 0800 BP 126/78, HR 88, RR 18, SpO₂ 97%; 1000 BP 98/60, HR 112, RR 24, SpO₂ 93%; 1200 BP 82/46, HR 132, RR 30, SpO₂ 88%. What is the priority interpretation?
items.content: Progressive hemodynamic and respiratory deterioration requiring immediate escalation.
items.rationale: Falling blood pressure and oxygen saturation with rising heart and respiratory rates indicate worsening perfusion and respiratory compromise. Activate rapid response rather than waiting for routine reassessment.

items.title: A septic client's urine output is 42 mL/hr at 0800, 25 mL/hr at 0900, 14 mL/hr at 1000, and 10 mL/hr at 1100; creatinine rises from 0.9 to 1.8 mg/dL. What should the nurse conclude?
items.content: Renal function and perfusion are worsening; urgent reassessment and escalation are needed.
items.rationale: Progressive oliguria with rising creatinine is concerning for acute kidney injury. Reassess hemodynamics, volume status, nephrotoxic exposures, and escalate promptly.

items.title: A 72-year-old with chronic heart failure reports two days of worsening orthopnea and a 2.4-kg weight gain. Assessment: BP 168/92 mm Hg, HR 112/min, RR 28/min, SpO₂ 88% on room air, crackles halfway up both lungs, and 3+ ankle edema. Which problem is the priority and what initial nursing actions are indicated?
items.content: Priority: acute pulmonary congestion with hypoxemia. Actions: position upright, provide prescribed oxygen, urgently notify the provider/rapid response based on severity, administer prescribed IV diuretic, and reassess respiratory status and urine output.
items.rationale: The weight gain, edema, crackles, orthopnea, and hypoxemia indicate acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary congestion. Oxygenation and work of breathing take priority while prescribed diuresis and close reassessment address fluid overload.
